findings.trigger: POST /api/watchdog/maintenance with a JSON body that omits 'minutes' (e.g. {"container": "nginx"}). The try block computes int(data.get('minutes', 0)) = 0 and pause() succeeds, actually pausing the container's automation. The very next line rebuilds the log message with int(data.get('minutes')) - this time with NO default - which raises TypeError on None and is not caught here, so Flask turns it into an unhandled 500. The client sees a server error and never gets {'success': True, 'until': ...}, even though the maintenance pause was already applied.
findings.suggestion: Parse minutes once into a local variable inside the try block and reuse that value for both pause() and the log message, instead of calling int(data.get('minutes')) a second time without the same default.

findings.trigger: POST /api/automation/test while the Flask worker thread has a running event loop (loop_running == True), and the rule-matching call in check_all_rules() (via automation_service._check_match) hangs or simply runs past 30 seconds. future.result(timeout=30) raises TimeoutError as intended, but that exception is raised while still inside 'with concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor() as executor:'. Leaving that block calls executor.__exit__, which runs shutdown(wait=True) - this does not cancel the still-running task, it blocks the request thread until that task actually finishes. The comment '# 30s timeout for safety' is therefore not true: the handler keeps blocking for as long as the hung check takes, with no actual bound.
findings.suggestion: Call executor.shutdown(wait=False) (or cancel/track the future explicitly) before letting the TimeoutError propagate, so exiting the with-block does not itself re-introduce an unbounded wait.

findings.trigger: Call edit_task(operation='update') for an existing task whose cycle is unchanged (e.g. 'monthly'), with data['schedule_details'] containing only the field(s) actually being changed, e.g. {'time': '08:00'} without 'day'/'month'/'year'. _update_task_schedule_details unconditionally sets task.day_val, task.month_val, task.year_val, task.weekday_val and task.cron_string to None first, then repopulates only the keys that are present in the incoming schedule_details dict - so day_val/month_val/year_val for this monthly task silently become None and the original day/month of the schedule is lost, with no error reported, changing (or breaking) when the task actually runs.
findings.suggestion: Only clear the fields that the incoming schedule_details is actually going to replace for the task's cycle, or require callers of edit_task/update to always send the complete schedule_details for the current cycle and validate that before clearing anything.
findings.unsure_why: The route that calls this (likely app/blueprints/tasks_bp.py) is outside this section, and the comment at :999 ('checked by the route (v3.1.0)') suggests the route may already guarantee a complete schedule_details payload for the task's cycle before calling into this service, in which case this path is unreachable in practice. It is also unclear whether task.is_valid() (defined in services/scheduling/scheduler.py, not in this section) would reject a task left with day_val=None for a non-cron cycle and surface a visible error instead of silently saving it - if it does, the practical impact is smaller (a visible failure instead of a silent one).

notes: Two minor points that did not rise to formal findings: (1) In TaskManagementService.list_tasks, when a task's forced deactivation write fails and the code restores task_data['is_active'] = True to reflect the file's real state (an existing, deliberate Z3 safeguard per the comments at :811-817), the row's 'frontend_status' field is left as computed before the restore (often 'expired'), so the panel could show is_active=True together with frontend_status='expired' for that one row until the next successful save - a display inconsistency, not a lost action. (2) app/auth.py, app/__init__.py and the rest of app/blueprints/automation_routes.py were read in full; no other defects matching the review criteria (silent tidying, drifting duplicate logic, right-function-wrong-call-site, over-promising comments) were found there. ScheduledTask, the scheduler module, tasks_bp.py, and the automation/config services that this section calls into are not part of this section and were not available to verify some of the downstream assumptions noted above.
